questions.q: In traditional currency, a trusted centralized party (like a bank) enforces account balances and transaction correctness. What does Bitcoin use instead?
choices: A smaller group of regional banks that audit each other
Cryptography, with no centralized party
A government-run registry of public keys
A single trusted server that stores the ledger
questions.explain: Bitcoin's goal is to provide the basic properties of a working currency without any centralized party. It uses cryptography to enforce them instead of a trusted entity.

questions.q: Which of these are properties of a functioning currency in the simplified model Bitcoin tries to replicate?
choices: Each person has an account that stores the units of currency they own
Alice cannot impersonate Bob and act as Bob
When Alice sends Bob n units, her balance drops by n and his rises by n
A user with n units cannot spend more than n units in a transaction
Every transaction must be approved by a designated authority
Account balances are hidden from all other users
questions.explain: The four properties are: accounts, no impersonation, transactions that move n units from sender to receiver, and no spending beyond your balance. Approval by an authority is exactly what Bitcoin avoids. Hidden balances are not a property, and in fact anyone can work out balances from the public ledger.

questions.q: What does it mean for a cryptographic hash H to be collision-resistant?
choices: Given H(x), it is infeasible to recover x
H always produces an output the same length as its input
It is infeasible to find two inputs x != y such that H(x) = H(y)
H(x) changes every time it is computed on the same x
questions.explain: Collision resistance means you can't feasibly find two different inputs that hash to the same output. Hash chains rely on this property: a modified block can't keep the same hash.

questions.q: A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary-length input to an output whose length grows with the input length.
questions.explain: A cryptographic hash maps arbitrary-length input to a fixed-length output.

questions.q: Alice signs a message. Which key does she use to create the signature, and which key do others use to verify it?
choices: She signs with her public key PK; others verify with her secret key SK
She signs with her secret key SK; others verify with her public key PK
She signs with the recipient's public key; the recipient verifies with their secret key
She signs and others verify with the same shared secret key
questions.explain: Alice keeps the secret signing key SK to herself and broadcasts the public verification key PK. She signs with SK, and anyone can check the signature with PK.

questions.q: With no central party keeping accounts, what serves as a user's identity in Bitcoin?
choices: Their secret signing key
A username registered with the miners
Their public key
The hash of their first transaction
questions.explain: Each user generates a key pair and publishes the public key. That public key (for example PK_B for Bob) is their identity.

questions.q: Why can't an attacker who doesn't know SK_B impersonate Bob (the user PK_B)?
choices: Miners keep a list of IP addresses tied to each public key
Digital signatures are unforgeable, so the attacker can't produce a signature that verifies under PK_B
PK_B is kept secret, so the attacker never learns Bob's identity
The hash chain records which computer each user is on
questions.explain: Bob proves he is PK_B by signing with SK_B. Without SK_B, the attacker can't make a signature that validates with PK_B, because signatures are unforgeable. PK_B is public, not secret.

questions.q: Alice wants to send n units to Bob. She writes the message "PK_A sends n units of currency to PK_B". Which key does she sign it with? (Use notation like PK_X / SK_X.)
questions.explain: The sender signs with her own secret key SK_A. Anyone can then verify the signature with PK_A and confirm that user PK_A intended the transaction.

questions.q: In Bitcoin, the recipient of a transaction must also sign it before the transaction is valid.
questions.explain: Bitcoin doesn't validate the recipient. If the recipient doesn't want the money, they can make another transaction to send it back.

questions.q: Bob receives 3 units from Alice that he doesn't want. What can he do in Bitcoin?
choices: Refuse to countersign, which cancels the transaction
Ask the miners to delete the transaction from the ledger
Create a new transaction that sends the money back to Alice
Nothing; the money is permanently locked in his account
questions.explain: The ledger is append-only, so a transaction can't be removed, and recipients aren't validated. To refuse money, the recipient creates a new transaction sending it back.

questions.q: Bitcoin's ledger explicitly stores each user's current balance.
questions.explain: Bitcoin doesn't record balances explicitly. It records every completed transaction with its signature, and anyone can work out any user's balance at any time from that history.

questions.q: Which pair of properties must the public ledger have?
choices: Private and editable
Append-only and immutable
Encrypted and deletable
Centralized and rewritable
questions.explain: Everyone can view the ledger and add new entries, but nobody can change or delete existing entries. It works like a guest book.

questions.q: Carol starts with 20 units and everyone else starts with 0. The ledger is: (1) Carol sends Dave 8. (2) Carol sends Erin 5. (3) Dave sends Erin 3. What is Erin's balance after these three transactions?
questions.explain: Erin receives 5 from Carol and 3 from Dave and spends nothing, so she has 8. (Carol has 7 and Dave has 5.)

questions.q: Carol starts with 12 units and everyone else starts with 0. Which transaction in this ledger is invalid?
choices: (1) Carol sends Dave 7
(2) Dave sends Erin 4
(3) Carol sends Erin 3
(4) Dave sends Frank 4
questions.explain: After (1): Carol 5, Dave 7. After (2): Dave 3, Erin 4. After (3): Carol 2, Erin 7. In (4), Dave tries to spend 4 but has only 3, so it's invalid.

questions.q: Which checks are part of validating a new transaction?
choices: The signature verifies under the sender's public key
The sender was the receiver in some earlier transaction
The sender hasn't already spent that money in an earlier transaction
The recipient has signed to accept the transaction
The signature verifies under the recipient's public key
A bank has confirmed the sender's balance
questions.explain: The three steps are: (1) check the signature with the sender's PK, (2) check that the sender received money in a previous transaction, and (3) check that the sender hasn't already spent it, so they have enough left. Recipients aren't validated, and there is no bank.

questions.q: TX_1: Bob sends Alice 5 (from his initial budget). TX_2: Alice sends Eve 5, citing TX_1. Later, Alice broadcasts TX_3: Alice sends Mallory 5, also citing TX_1. Which validation check does TX_3 fail?
choices: The signature check, because Alice's signature can't be verified
The check that the sender was the receiver in an earlier transaction
The check that the money hasn't already been spent in an earlier transaction
None; TX_3 is valid because TX_1 really did pay Alice
questions.explain: Alice really was the receiver in TX_1, and she can sign validly. But scanning the history shows that the money from TX_1 was already used in TX_2, so TX_3 is trying to spend it a second time.

questions.q: Why does each transaction record which earlier transaction its money came from (for example, TX_2 says its money came from TX_1)?
choices: So the recipient can decide whether to accept the money
So verifiers can confirm the sender received those funds and hasn't already spent them
So the transaction can be encrypted under the earlier transaction's key
So miners know which user to charge a fee
questions.explain: Pointing to the source lets anyone check that the sender received the money and that it hasn't been spent elsewhere. This is also why blocks have to be kept in order of creation.

questions.q: Assuming a trusted append-only ledger that everyone can read, users can't spend more than their balance, because anyone can compute every balance from the ledger and reject overspending.
questions.explain: Since the full transaction history is public and can't be changed, any overspending attempt can be detected and rejected.

questions.q: In a hash chain holding messages m_1 ... m_5, what does Block 3 contain?
choices: m_3 only
m_3 and H(Block 2)
m_3 and H(Block 4)
H(m_1), H(m_2) and m_3
questions.explain: Each block after the first holds its message plus the hash of the previous block. Block 1 holds only m_1.

questions.q: Fully expanded, what is Block 4 of a hash chain?
questions.explain: Block 4 = m_4, H(Block 3) = m_4, H(m_3, H(Block 2)) = m_4, H(m_3, H(m_2, H(Block 1))) = m_4, H(m_3, H(m_2, H(m_1))).

questions.q: In a five-block hash chain, which messages does H(Block 3) commit to (act as a digest of)?
questions.explain: Block 3 contains m_3 and H(Block 2), which in turn covers m_2 and H(Block 1) = H(m_1). So H(Block 3) is a digest of m_1, m_2 and m_3. Later blocks aren't included.

questions.q: To verify a hash chain of blocks 1 through i downloaded from an untrusted server, Alice needs a trusted copy of the hash of every block.
questions.explain: She only needs H(Block i), the hash of the latest block, from a trusted source. She recomputes each block's hash, checks it against the hash stored in the next block, and finally compares H(Block i) with the trusted value.

questions.q: Alice gets H(Block 4) from a trusted source and downloads blocks 1-4 from a compromised server. The attacker replaces Block 2 with Block 2' and updates every later block so the stored hashes match. Why does Alice still catch the attack?
choices: Block 2' has an invalid digital signature
The change carries forward: Block 3' holds H(Block 2'), Block 4' holds H(Block 3'), so H(Block 4') doesn't equal the trusted H(Block 4)
The attacker can't change Block 3, so H(Block 2') is left unreferenced
Alice compares Block 2' with a trusted copy of Block 2
questions.explain: Because of collision resistance, H(Block 2') != H(Block 2). Block 3 must then change to hold the new hash, so H(Block 3') != H(Block 3), and so on up to H(Block 4') != H(Block 4). The mismatch with the trusted hash reveals the tampering.

questions.q: An attacker modifies Block 2 into Block 2' but leaves Block 3 unchanged, so Block 3 still holds the original H(Block 2). How does Alice detect this while checking the chain?
choices: The recomputed H(Block 2') doesn't match the hash stored in Block 3
Block 3's message no longer decrypts correctly
H(Block 1) stored in Block 2' is now wrong
She can't detect it, because Block 3 is unchanged
questions.explain: Alice recomputes each block's hash and checks it against the hash stored in the next block. Since H(Block 2') != H(Block 2), the check against Block 3 fails right away.

questions.q: Which property of the hash function guarantees that a tampered block can't have the same hash as the original?
choices: Fixed output length
Collision resistance
Fast computation
Being keyed with a secret
questions.explain: Collision resistance makes it infeasible to find a different block with the same hash, so any change to a block changes its hash.

questions.q: If you get the hash of the latest block from a trusted source, you can verify that all earlier history in the hash chain is correct.
questions.explain: This is the key property of a hash chain. The latest block's hash commits, through the chain of hashes, to every earlier block.

questions.q: In Bitcoin, every participant stores the entire blockchain.
questions.explain: There is no centralized server, so every participant keeps the full blockchain and its history. New transactions are broadcast to everyone for checking.

questions.q: What is a fork in a blockchain?
choices: A transaction that sends money to two recipients
Different versions of the blockchain that exist at the same time
A block that contains two proofs of work
A copy of the blockchain stored by a single miner
questions.explain: A fork is when different versions of the blockchain exist at the same time, for example after someone builds a new chain starting from an earlier point.

questions.q: Mallory buys a house from Bob for 500 units, and the transaction is added to the ledger. She then builds a new chain starting just before that transaction. What is she trying to do?
choices: Speed up confirmation of the payment
Get other users to accept a chain without the payment, so she gets her 500 units back
Make Bob's identity invalid
Recover Bob's secret key from the old block
questions.explain: By 'going back in time' and forking from before the payment, Mallory hopes others will accept a history where she never paid. That would get her 500 units back. Consensus is needed to stop this.

questions.q: Who is allowed to append a new block to the Bitcoin blockchain?
choices: Any user who stores the blockchain
Only the sender of the transactions in the block
Miners who have a valid proof of work
Users chosen by majority vote
questions.explain: Every user stores the chain, but only miners can add blocks, and only with a valid proof of work. A miner validates transactions, then tries to solve the proof of work before other miners.

questions.q: When is a Bitcoin proof of work considered solved?
choices: When the hash of the block concatenated with a random number starts with N zero bits
When the block's hash equals the previous block's hash
When a majority of users sign the block
When the random number reaches N
questions.explain: The puzzle hashes the current block concatenated with a random number. The proof of work is solved when the resulting hash starts with N zero bits, where N (for example 33) is set by the Bitcoin algorithm.

questions.q: While mining, what does a miner change in order to search for a valid proof of work?
choices: The transactions' signatures
The hash of the previous block
The random number concatenated with the block, which is incremented to change the hash
The value of N
questions.explain: The miner keeps incrementing the random number. Each new value gives a different hash, and the miner continues until the hash starts with N zero bits.

questions.q: Honest miners hear about several competing chains. Which one do they accept?
choices: The longest correct chain
The chain they heard about first
The chain whose latest block has the most zero bits
The chain with the most transactions in its newest block
questions.explain: The key idea for consensus is that everyone always prefers the longest correct chain. Other versions are discarded.

questions.q: If a miner broadcasts a chain that is longer than everyone else's but contains a block with an incorrect transaction, honest miners adopt it because the longest chain always wins.
questions.explain: Honest miners accept the longest correct chain. A block with an incorrect transaction is ignored.

questions.q: Honest miner M1 holds b1->b2->b3->b4 and is mining b5. It then hears a valid broadcast b1->b2->b3->b4'->b5'. What does M1 do?
choices: Keep its own chain because it accepted b4 first
Merge b4 and b4' into one block
Discard its shorter chain, adopt b1->b2->b3->b4'->b5', and mine on top of b5'
Ignore both chains and wait for a majority vote
questions.explain: The longer correct chain wins, so M1 drops b1->b2->b3->b4 in favor of b1->b2->b3->b4'->b5'. Always accepting the longest chain keeps all miners' views the same.

questions.q: Two miners solve a proof of work at the same time and append different blocks, forking the network. How is the fork resolved?
choices: The block with the smaller hash value wins
The next miner to append onto one of the chains makes it longer, which invalidates the other
Both chains are kept permanently and merged later
The two miners must split the block between them
questions.explain: When the next block is appended to one branch, that branch becomes the longest, and the other version is discarded.

questions.q: What assumption does Bitcoin's consensus rely on?
choices: No user ever behaves maliciously
Miners are vetted by a central authority
More than half of the computing power belongs to honest miners
Every user has the same amount of computing power
questions.explain: Bitcoin assumes most users are honest, meaning that more than half of the computing power belongs to honest miners. That gives the honest miners the advantage in building the longest chain.

questions.q: With proof-of-work consensus in place, why does Mallory's attempt to fork away her 500-unit house payment fail?
choices: Her forked blocks have invalid signatures
Without more than 50% of the world's computing power, she can't mine faster than everyone else, so her fork stays shorter and is rejected
Bob can delete her forked blocks from the ledger
The hash chain stops anyone from creating blocks after an old block
questions.explain: Only the longest chain is accepted. Mallory's fork would only win if she could mine new blocks faster than all the other miners combined, and that requires more than 50% of the computing power.

questions.q: Which of these are ways the text says malicious users in the network might misbehave?
choices: Not appending certain transactions
Not checking certain transactions correctly
Replaying certain transactions
Allowing invalid transactions
questions.explain: All four are listed: refusing to append transactions, checking them incorrectly, replaying them, and allowing invalid ones. Bitcoin copes with these by assuming most users are honest.
